title: The arabesque
hookLine: endless vines and leaves, growing without beginning or end

cards: A strip of carved plaster runs along the top of a wall, no wider than a hand. A stem curls left, splits, and sends out a leaf. The leaf turns into another stem.
That stem curls right, splits again, and sends out half a palm leaf, which turns into yet another stem. Follow it and you never find the root, or the last leaf.
At the corner the strip just stops, cut off by its frame, as if the vine carries on behind the plaster. It isn't a picture of a plant from any garden. It's a plant that only grows.

teach.b: The arabesque turns up in mosque plaster, on palace walls, in the borders of handwritten books, on the lids of metal bowls: stems that split, curl and rejoin, leaves that turn into new stems.
Yesterday's geometry was ruled lines and compass circles locking into stars. The arabesque is a living curve. One is crystal; the other is growth.
Look at what the artist leaves out.
No root to point at, and no flower at the end that says, here, it's finished. Some readers see in it a picture the Qur'an itself draws, a likeness for good speech.

teach.h: A GOODLY SAYING, A GOODLY TREE.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "A goodly saying, as a goodly tree, its root set firm, its branches reaching into heaven." The next verse adds that it gives its fruit at every season, by permission of its Lord.
Here the two part ways. The vine on the wall hides its root; the verse insists on one. A good word stands firm underneath, and that's why it can keep bearing fruit above.
Nobody can show that an artist carved a vine to illustrate that verse, but it's a fair thing to remember while standing under one.
And the vine has a practical gift: it fills any shape. A dome, a window arch, the border of a page of the Qur'an, the lid of a box.
The same few moves, stem, split, curl, leaf, can wrap around anything, sometimes around calligraphy, so the words sit inside a garden of their own.

how: Arabesque vines appear in mosque plaster and tile, in the borders of Qur'an manuscripts and on metalwork, often around calligraphy; craftspeople in places such as Iran, Turkey and Morocco still draw and carve them by hand.

games.q: you're carving a vine along a wall, and you reach the corner. what do you do with the line?
o: finish it with one big flower.
let the frame cut it off, as if it carries on.
curl it back to where it began.
games.why: the frame stops it. with no root and no last leaf, the eye reads the vine as growing on past the edge.

practice: In the margin of any page, start a line in the middle, not at the edge, and let it curl.
When it wants to, split it in two, give one half a leaf, and let the leaf become a new stem, slowly, without planning and without drawing an ending.
If you pray, let each curl carry a quiet remembrance of God; if you don't, just watch the line grow.

wordCard.voice: The arabesque. A carved or painted vine with no root and no last leaf, curling and splitting to fill any shape. Today's word.
